doc.title: Al Chez interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, February 13, 2019

title: Wanting to sound like Al Chez; Louis Armstrong as favorite
summary: Chez names Louis Armstrong as his favorite trumpeter for his unique sound and says he wants to develop his own, ever-evolving sound.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: my soul, it goes through everything, and what comes out, every time I play, is something unique and different. And I embrace that too. I don’t want to really — how do I put this the right way? I don’t want to duplicate anything that I’ve done before because I’ve done that already. You know what I mean? So when I’m playing, every note, every solo, every phrase has its own — a life of its own. And I kind of dig that. You know what I mean? My favorite trumpet player is Louis Armstrong. Not because — well a couple of reasons. Louis Armstrong — there’s never been another trumpet player to really duplicate that sound that he has. There’s guys that sound like Maynard Ferguson. There’s guys that sound like Doc Severinsen. There’s guys that sound like Roy Hargrove. There’s guys that sound like, you know, Wynton Marsalis. But there’s been nobody who’s really duplicated that Louis Armstrong kind of vibe, probably because he created that whole sound of his and he embraced the uniqueness. You know it’s like he wasn’t going to try to sound like this guy or this guy or this guy, he was going to try to sound like Louis Armstrong. And I kind of do that same thing. I don’t want to sound like Maynard Ferguson, I don’t want to sound like Bill Chase, I don’t want to sound like Louis Armstrong. I want to sound like Al Chez. You know? And I want to hone my sound and I want to get it so that it goes through my soul properly and then every time I play something I want to change that a little bit. I want to keep working on, you know, that sound. Like that’s the main thing for me, keep on working on my sound and my sound keeps evolving you know. Kind of like somebody who is learning. The smartest man in the world, the first thing he’s going to tell you is I don’t know everything. So he’s going to keep learning. I’m going to keep evolving with my sound and have my sound keep on evolving. Now whether that’s song to song, whether that’s phrase to phrase, whether that’s solo to solo, or measure to measure, or note to note, it keeps evolving. And I kind of dig that.
